blocks.html:
READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Carnivorous plants

They attract insects and then eat their flesh. Is that any way for a plant to behave?

The naturalist and author of On the Origin of Species, Charles Darwin, was fascinated by carnivorous plants. In 1860, soon after he came across his first carnivorous plant — the sundew, Drosera — he wrote, 'I care more about Drosera than the origin of all the species in the world.' He spent months running experiments on the plants. He dropped flies and bits of meat on their leaves and watched them slowly fold their sticky tentacles over their prey. He thought it incredible that brushing a leaf with a single strand of human hair was enough to bring about a response. Yet sundews, he observed, ignored raindrops. To react to such a false alarm, he reasoned, would obviously be a great evil to the plant. This was no accident. This was adaptation.

Darwin expanded his studies from sundews to other species in his book Insectivorous Plants. He was amazed at the quickness and power of the Venus flytrap. He showed that when one of its leaves snapped shut, it formed itself into a temporary ‘stomach', secreting enzymes that could dissolve the prey. He noted that a leaf took more than a week to reopen after closing, and reasoned that the interlocking spines along the margin of the leaf allowed tiny insects to escape, saving the plant the expense of digesting an insufficient meal.

Today, biologists using 21st-century tools to study cells and DNA are beginning to understand how these plants hunt, eat, and digest — and how these strange adaptations came about in the first place. Alexander Volkov, a plant physiologist at Oakwood University in Alabama, believes he has figured out the Venus flytrap's secret. ‘This,' Volkov declares, 'is an electrical plant.'

When an insect brushes against a hair on the leaf of a Venus flytrap, the movement sets off an electric charge. The charge builds up inside the tissue of the leaf but is not enough to stimulate the snap, which keeps the Venus flytrap from reacting to false alarms, such as raindrops. An insect, however, is likely to brush a second hair, adding enough electric charge for the leaf to close.

Volkov's experiments reveal that the electric charge travels down fluid-filled tunnels in a leaf, which opens up pores in cell membranes. Water rushes from the cells on the inside of the leaf to those on the outside, causing the leaf to rapidly flip in shape from convex to concave, like a soft contact lens. As the leaves flip, they snap together, trapping an insect inside.

The bladderwort plant has an equally sophisticated way of setting its underwater trap. It pumps water out of tiny air sacs or bladders, lowering the pressure inside. When a water flea or some other small creature swims past, it bends hairs on the bladder, causing a flap to spring apart. The low pressure sucks water in, carrying the creature along with it. In one five-hundredth of a second, the flap swings shut again. The cells in the bladder then begin to pump water out again, creating a new vacuum. Many other species of carnivorous plants act like living flypaper, catching animals on sticky tentacles. Pitcher plants use yet another strategy, growing long tube-shaped leaves into which insects fall. Some of the largest have pitchers up to 30cm deep and can consume whole frogs unlucky enough to fall into them. Sophisticated chemistry helps make the pitcher a death trap.

Nicholas Gotelli, of the University of Vermont, is trying to figure out what evolutionary forces pushed these plants towards meat. Carnivorous plants clearly benefit from eating animals; when scientists feed pitcher plants extra bugs, the plants get bigger. But the benefits of eating flesh are not the ones you might expect. Carnivorous animals, like ourselves, use the carbon in protein and the fat in meat to build muscles and store energy. Carnivorous plants, however, take nitrogen and phosphorus from the flesh in order to build light-harvesting enzymes. Eating animals, in other words, lets carnivorous plants do what all plants do: grow by taking energy directly from the sun.

Unfortunately, they do a really bad job of it. That's because they have to use a lot of energy to make the equipment they need to catch animals — the enzymes, the pumps, the sticky tentacles, and so on. A pitcher or a flytrap is not very good at photosynthesis because, unlike plants with ordinary leaves, it does not have flat solar panels that can absorb lots of sunlight. Gotelli suspects that only under special conditions are the benefits of being carnivorous greater than the costs. The poor soil of bogs and swamps, where many carnivorous plants grow, offers little nitrogen and phosphorus, so carnivorous plants enjoy an advantage there over ‘conventional' plants. Also, bogs are often flooded with sunshine, so even an inefficient carnivorous plant can carry out enough photosynthesis to survive. 'They're stuck, and they're making the best of it,' says Aaron Ellison of Harvard University.

Unfortunately, the adaptations that enable carnivorous plants to survive in harsh habitats also make them extremely sensitive to environmental changes. Chemical fertilizers used in agriculture and pollution from power plants are adding extra nitrogen to many bogs in North America. Carnivorous plants are so finely adapted to low levels of nitrogen that this extra fertilizer is overloading their systems. Humans also threaten carnivorous plants in other ways. The black market trade in exotic carnivorous plants is strong, but even if this can be prevented, carnivorous plants will continue to suffer from other dangers. Their habitat is disappearing, to be replaced by shopping centers and houses. The suppression of wildfires by government agencies allows other plants to grow quickly and outcompete the Venus flytraps. Good news, perhaps, for flies. But a loss for all who delight in the inventiveness of evolution.

questionGroups.bodyHtml:
Complete the notes below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

Carnivorous Plants

Darwin's experiments:

Drosera

  • He put insects and small amounts of meat onto leaves and observed what happened.
  • He was amazed that one human hair triggered a response.
  • He understood why the plant did not respond to 1 .

Venus flytrap

  • He demonstrated how leaves close and then, for a short period, act like a 2 .
  • He noted the structure of the leaves ensures small insects are released.

Biology today:

Venus flytrap

  • If insects come into contact with leaf hairs, their movement produces an electric charge.
  • The charge enters fluid-filled tunnels, causing 3 in cell membranes to open.
  • Water moves between cells and then the leaf changes from convex to concave, trapping the insect inside.

Bladderwort

  • Hairs bend when insects swim past, resulting in the opening of a flap.
  • Water is sucked in.
  • When water is pumped out of bladder cells, a 4 builds up inside.

Pitcher plants

  • The plants have tube-shaped leaves that insects fall into.
  • Some plants are big enough to capture and eat 5 .

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?

In boxes 6–13 on your answer sheet, write:

  • TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
  • FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
  • NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

6 Pitcher plants increase in size after they have digested a lot of insects.

7 Carnivorous plants produce light-harvesting enzymes with the nutrients they extract from animals.

8 Pitcher plants and Venus flytraps are more efficient at photosynthesis than plants with ordinary leaves.

9 Venus flytraps are better adapted to the soil of swamps and bogs than other carnivorous plants.

10 Carnivorous plants frequently find it difficult to photosynthesise in bogs due to a lack of sunlight.

11 Scientists have campaigned to reduce the amount of nitrogen that is released into the soil by agricultural practices.

12 A lot of exotic carnivorous plants are sold illegally.

13 Preventing wildfires is beneficial to the Venus flytrap.

passageNotes.label: Paragraph A
passageNotes.text: 博物学家查尔斯·达尔文对食虫植物十分着迷。1860年，他发现第一株茅膏菜后，进行了数月实验：把苍蝇和肉屑放到叶片上，观察黏性腺毛慢慢包住猎物。他还发现，一根人类头发就足以引发叶片反应，而雨滴却不会触发反应，因为对这种错误信号作出反应会给植物带来不必要的消耗。这不是偶然现象，而是植物的适应。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph B
passageNotes.text: 达尔文在《食虫植物》一书中把研究扩展到其他物种。他惊叹捕蝇草闭合的速度和力量，并证明叶片闭合后会暂时形成“胃”，分泌能够溶解猎物的酶。叶片边缘相互咬合的刺允许微小昆虫逃脱，避免植物为一顿不足量的食物付出消化成本。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph C
passageNotes.text: 如今，生物学家借助研究细胞和 DNA 的工具，开始理解食虫植物如何捕猎、进食和消化，以及这些奇特适应性最初是如何形成的。阿拉巴马州奥克伍德大学的植物生理学家亚历山大·沃尔科夫认为自己已经揭开了捕蝇草的秘密：这是一种“带电的植物”。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph D
passageNotes.text: 当昆虫碰到捕蝇草叶片上的毛时，运动会产生电荷。电荷在叶片组织中积累，但第一次触碰的电量不足以使叶片闭合，从而避免对雨滴等错误信号作出反应；昆虫通常还会碰到第二根毛，电荷增加到足以使叶片关闭。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph E
passageNotes.text: 沃尔科夫的实验表明，电荷会沿叶片中充满液体的通道传播，并打开细胞膜上的孔。叶片内侧细胞中的水流向外侧细胞，使叶片像柔软的隐形眼镜一样迅速由凸面翻成凹面；叶片翻转时合拢，把昆虫困在里面。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph F
passageNotes.text: 狸藻有同样复杂的水下捕猎方式。它先把微小气囊中的水抽出，降低囊内压力；当水蚤等小生物游过时，会碰弯气囊上的毛，使盖片弹开。低压把水和猎物一起吸入，盖片在五百分之一秒内重新关闭，气囊细胞随后再次抽水，形成新的真空。其他食虫植物则像活的捕蝇纸，用黏性腺毛捕捉动物；猪笼草长出管状叶片，使昆虫落入其中，有些甚至能捕食整只青蛙。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph G
passageNotes.text: 佛蒙特大学的尼古拉斯·戈泰利试图弄清哪些进化力量促使植物走向食肉。食虫植物显然能从捕食动物中获益，额外喂食昆虫的猪笼草会长得更大。但它们获取的并不是动物用来长肌肉和储存能量的碳和脂肪，而是利用肉中的氮和磷来制造捕光酶，从而完成所有植物都要做的事：直接从太阳获取能量生长。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph H
passageNotes.text: 然而，食虫植物为了制造捕猎所需的酶、泵和黏性腺毛，需要消耗大量能量，因此捕食的收益通常不足以抵消成本。猪笼草和捕蝇草的光合作用效率也不如拥有平展叶片的普通植物。只有在特殊环境中，食肉的收益才可能超过成本：沼泽和湿地土壤缺少氮、磷，而阳光通常充足，所以食虫植物在这些地方反而具有优势。

passageNotes.label: Paragraph I
passageNotes.text: 使食虫植物适应恶劣栖息地的特征，也让它们对环境变化极为敏感。农业化肥和发电厂污染给北美许多沼泽增加了氮，使这些高度适应低氮环境的植物系统超负荷。黑市上的异域食虫植物交易也很活跃；此外，它们的栖息地正被购物中心和住宅取代，政府压制野火还让其他植物快速生长并挤压捕蝇草。

items.text:
题目：He understood why the plant did not respond to ______.
题目翻译：他理解了为什么这种植物不会对 ______ 作出反应。
答案：raindrops
解析：定位 Paragraph A，原文："Yet sundews, he observed, ignored raindrops." 达尔文观察到茅膏菜会忽略雨滴，这可避免对假信号的无效反应。

题目：Venus flytrap leaves close and then act like a temporary ______.
题目翻译：捕蝇草叶片闭合后会暂时像一个 ______ 一样工作。
答案：stomach
解析：定位 Paragraph B，原文："he showed that when one of its leaves snapped shut, it formed itself into a temporary 'stomach'"。达尔文证明叶片闭合后形成临时“胃”，分泌酶消化猎物。

题目：The charge causes ______ in cell membranes to open.
题目翻译：电荷会导致细胞膜中的 ______ 打开。
答案：pores
解析：定位 Paragraph E，原文："which opens up pores in cell membranes"。Volkov 的实验显示电信号沿液体通道传递并触发膜孔开启，水分随之转移。

题目：When water is pumped out of bladder cells, a ______ builds up inside.
题目翻译：当囊泡细胞把水抽出后，内部会形成 ______。
答案：vacuum
解析：定位 Paragraph F，原文："The cells in the bladder then begin to pump water out again, creating a new vacuum." 狸藻通过抽水降低囊内压力，形成真空状态以便快速吸入猎物。

题目：Some pitcher plants are big enough to capture and eat ______.
题目翻译：一些猪笼草大到足以捕获并吞食 ______。
答案：frogs
解析：定位 Paragraph F，原文："Some of the largest have pitchers up to 30cm deep and can consume whole frogs..." 最大类型的捕虫囊深达 30 厘米，可吞食整只青蛙。

questionExplanations.text: 题目 1-5 答案依次为：raindrops, stomach, pores, vacuum, frogs。

items.text:
题目：Pitcher plants increase in size after they have digested a lot of insects.
题目翻译：猪笼草在消化大量昆虫后会变大。
答案：TRUE
解析：定位 Paragraph G，原文："when scientists feed pitcher plants extra bugs, the plants get bigger." 这直接支持题干所述现象。

题目：Carnivorous plants produce light-harvesting enzymes with the nutrients they extract from animals.
题目翻译：食虫植物利用从动物体内获取的营养来构建光捕获酶。
答案：TRUE
解析：定位 Paragraph G，原文："Carnivorous plants... take nitrogen and phosphorus from the flesh in order to build light-harvesting enzymes." 题干与原文一致。

题目：Pitcher plants and Venus flytraps are more efficient at photosynthesis than plants with ordinary leaves.
题目翻译：猪笼草和捕蝇草的光合作用效率高于普通叶片植物。
答案：FALSE
解析：定位 Paragraph H，原文："A pitcher or a flytrap is not very good at photosynthesis because... it does not have flat solar panels..." 这些捕食结构并不利于光合作用，效率低于普通平展叶片。

题目：Venus flytraps are better adapted to the soil of swamps and bogs than other carnivorous plants.
题目翻译：捕蝇草比其他食虫植物更适应沼泽土壤。
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：定位 Paragraph H，原文："The poor soil of bogs and swamps... so carnivorous plants enjoy an advantage there over 'conventional' plants." 文章只讨论食虫植物整体相对于普通植物的优势，没有给出捕蝇草与其他食虫植物的对比结论，因此为 NOT GIVEN。

题目：Carnivorous plants frequently find it difficult to photosynthesise in bogs due to a lack of sunlight.
题目翻译：食虫植物在沼泽中常因缺乏阳光而难以进行光合作用。
答案：FALSE
解析：定位 Paragraph H，原文："Also, bogs are often flooded with sunshine..." 沼泽往往阳光充足，不是缺光；它们的问题主要是捕食结构本身光合效率低。

题目：Scientists have campaigned to reduce the amount of nitrogen that is released into the soil by agricultural practices.
题目翻译：科学家已发起行动，减少农业向土壤释放氮。
答案：NOT GIVEN
解析：定位 Paragraph I，原文："Chemical fertilizers used in agriculture... are adding extra nitrogen..." 文章提到农业化肥增加了氮输入并伤害食虫植物，但未提到科学家开展了减少氮排放的“运动/行动”。

题目：A lot of exotic carnivorous plants are sold illegally.
题目翻译：大量异域食虫植物通过非法渠道交易。
答案：TRUE
解析：定位 Paragraph I，原文："The black market trade in exotic carnivorous plants is strong"，说明异域食虫植物存在规模显著的非法交易。

题目：Preventing wildfires is beneficial to the Venus flytrap.
题目翻译：抑制野火对捕蝇草有益。
答案：FALSE
解析：定位 Paragraph I，原文："The suppression of wildfires... allows other plants to grow quickly and outcompete the Venus flytraps." 抑制野火会让其他植物快速生长并挤压捕蝇草，结果是负面影响。

questionExplanations.text: 题目 6-13 答案依次为：TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, NOT GIVEN, FALSE, NOT GIVEN, TRUE, FALSE。
